retro_intro_puzzle.display_text: Welcome to the night sky. Around you are the constellations of the ecliptic: Leo, Virgo, Libra, and Scorpio. Watch the red point of Mars closely as we fast-forward through six months of sky-watching.

retro_eastward_drift.display_text: For the first two months, Mars drifts slowly eastward against the background stars, moving from near Leo toward Virgo.
retro_eastward_drift.llm_text: For the first two months, Mars drifts slowly eastward against the background stars, moving from near Leo toward Virgo.

retro_westward_loop.display_text: Now Mars slows, halts, and begins moving backward — westward — for about two months, tracing a loop roughly 15 degrees across.
retro_westward_loop.llm_text: Now Mars slows, halts, and begins moving backward — westward — for about two months, tracing a loop roughly fifteen degrees across.

retro_resume_eastward.display_text: Finally, Mars slows again, reverses once more, and resumes its normal eastward journey toward Libra and beyond.
retro_resume_eastward.llm_text: Finally, Mars slows again, reverses once more, and resumes its normal eastward journey toward Libra and beyond.

geocentric_intro.display_text: In the geocentric model, Earth sits fixed at the center. Mars rides on a small circle called the epicycle, which itself rides on a larger circle called the deferent, centered on Earth.
geocentric_intro.llm_text: In the geocentric model, Earth sits fixed at the center. Mars rides on a small circle called the epicycle, which itself rides on a larger circle called the deferent, centered on Earth.
geocentric_intro.spoken_text: In the geocentric model, Earth sits fixed at the center. Mars rides on a small circle called the epicycle, which itself rides on a larger circle called the deferent, centered on Earth.

geocentric_machinery_runs.display_text: Watch as the machinery runs. The epicycle carries Mars around while the whole system also revolves along the deferent.
geocentric_machinery_runs.llm_text: Watch as the machinery runs. The epicycle carries Mars around while the whole system also revolves along the deferent.
geocentric_machinery_runs.spoken_text: Watch as the machinery runs. The epicycle carries Mars around while the whole system also revolves along the deferent.

geocentric_retrograde_moment.display_text: Notice that when Mars reaches the inner part of its epicycle — the side closest to Earth — its combined motion makes it appear to move backward as seen from Earth. This model works, but requires carefully tuned circle sizes and speeds, and more epicycles had to be stacked on top as observations improved.

heliocentric_lift_up.display_text: Let's lift up out of the ecliptic plane to view the solar system from outside. The Sun sits at the center. Earth orbits at 1 astronomical unit with a period of one year; Mars orbits at 1.52 AU with a period of 1.88 years.

heliocentric_orbits_run.display_text: Watch the two planets run their orbits at correct relative speeds. Earth, on the faster inner orbit, gradually catches up to Mars.

heliocentric_overtake.display_text: Here comes the overtake — roughly every 26 months, Earth swings past Mars on its inner, faster orbit. This is the same event that produced the retrograde loop, but from here there are no epicycles needed — just two smooth ellipses.

linkage_intro.display_text: Now let's link the two perspectives. On the left, the heliocentric model; on the right, Earth's night sky. A line drawn from Earth through Mars extends out to the background stars.

linkage_eastward_sweep.display_text: During Mars's normal motion, this line-of-sight sweeps eastward through the constellations, matching Mars's normal eastward drift.
linkage_eastward_sweep.llm_text: During Mars's normal motion, this line-of-sight sweeps eastward through the constellations, matching Mars's normal eastward drift.

linkage_westward_reversal.display_text: As Earth begins to overtake Mars, the line reverses direction and sweeps westward — and at this exact moment, Mars's apparent position in the night sky retraces its path.
linkage_westward_reversal.llm_text: As Earth begins to overtake Mars, the line reverses direction and sweeps westward — and at this exact moment, Mars's apparent position in the night sky retraces its path.

linkage_resume_eastward.display_text: After Earth has passed Mars, the line resumes its eastward sweep. This is a real apparent motion produced by the geometry, not an illusion or a flaw in the eye.

embodied_intro.display_text: You are now standing at the center of a starfield with a stationary Mars in front of you. A small circle on the floor marks Earth's orbit. Walk slowly along it while keeping your eyes on Mars against the distant stars.

embodied_drift_phase.display_text: As you traverse the inner orbit, notice Mars's apparent position drifting across the constellations.

recap_intro.display_text: Let's recap what we've learned about apparent retrograde motion, covering five key concept areas.

recap_phenomenon_and_geocentric.display_text: First, we observed the phenomenon itself: Mars drifting eastward, looping westward, then resuming eastward motion. Then we saw the geocentric explanation, with Mars riding an epicycle on a deferent to produce the loop.

recap_heliocentric_and_linkage.display_text: Next, the heliocentric resolution showed the loop emerging naturally from Earth overtaking Mars, with no epicycles needed. We then linked the outside view to the night sky, seeing the line of sight sweep and reverse in step with Mars's apparent path.

recap_comparison_close.display_text: Finally, we compared Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn, seeing that more distant planets produce smaller retrograde loops. This full arc — from puzzling observation to elegant heliocentric explanation — is one of the great triumphs of astronomical reasoning.
